Need to search first.I've written notes on Psalm 93 from 20 pages, listed below. My research tools hit their usage limit partway through, so several sources you asked for are missing. I couldn't read Gill, Ellicott or the Pulpit Commentary as separate pages, and I got no Precept Austin page or NET Bible notes for v. 4–5. I found nothing at all on Lutheran, Methodist/Wesleyan, Pentecostal or Anglican sites, nothing on Bible Odyssey, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Those sections are left out, as you asked. Most notes come from the summaries the search tool returned rather than full pages.

**Sources**

- [2] https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps093.cfm (Spurgeon) and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-93.html (Treasury of David)
- [3] https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/93-1.htm (several older commentaries on one page)
- [4] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-93.html (Calvin)
- [5] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-93.html (Coffman)
- [6] https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/93-1.html, …/93-3.html, …/93-4.html (Barnes, Constable, Henry, Clarke)
- [7] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-93.html (Expositor's Bible)
- [8] https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_093.cfm (Matthew Henry)
- [9] https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-93.html (Preacher's Homiletical Commentary)

- [12] https://www.oca.org/files/PDF/Music/Rubrics/Horologion/office-vespers.pdf and https://www.oca.org/liturgics/outlines/little-vespers (Orthodox services)

- [14] https://biblehub.com/q/Psalm_93_3_and_ancient_divine_power.htm
- [15] https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-93
- [16] https://biblehub.com/psalms/93.htm (Bible Hub chapter summary)

---

**Whole psalm**
- Boice (quoted by Guzik) sees Psalm 93 as the first of several "theocratic" psalms. Their watchword is "Yahweh reigns." [1]
- Spurgeon notes that even Jewish interpreters linked these psalms to the times of the Messiah. [2]
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the Jews applied this psalm and the next six to the Messiah's times. [3]
- Constable calls it an "enthronement" psalm. He says these psalms focus on God's rule over Israel but also point ahead to the Messiah's reign in the Millennium. [6] (This end-times reading is distinctive to him; the other sources don't make the Millennium link.)
- Maclaren (Expositor's Bible) calls it the "overture" that sets the theme for the group of psalms that follows. [7]
- NET summary: God is king of the universe, keeping order and holding back destructive forces. [10]

**v. 1**
- **"The LORD reigns."**
  - The Hebrew stresses that it is Yahweh, and no other god, who rules (VanGemeren, quoted by Guzik). [1]
  - Spurgeon reads "reigns" with no limits: it covers God's rule over both the world and the church. [2]
- **Did God reign before, or "become king" here?**
  - Maclaren reads the verb as an action: "Jehovah has become King" through some recent act of power. This doesn't mean He wasn't king before (v. 2 rules that out). [7]
  - Hengstenberg (quoted in the Treasury of David and the Homiletical Commentary) says the verse means a new, glorious display of God's rule, not His everyday government. It echoes the cry that announced a new king (2 Sam 15:10; 2 Kgs 9:13). [2][9]
  - An older note on Bible Hub says God seemed to have set His rule aside for a time and now steps forward. It may point to a recent act of God, or ahead to the Messiah's reign. [3]
- **Robed and girded.**
  - Henry: majesty is a prince's robe at court, strength is a general's armour in camp. His power comes from no one else. [8]
  - A note on Bible Hub says putting on the robe and the sword were part of crowning a king. It compares Isa 59:17 and 63:1, where God appears as a warrior. [3]
  - Calvin: "clothing" does not mean God gets anything from outside Himself. It means His wisdom and justice become visible in how He governs. [4]
  - Spurgeon: God is always strong, but at times He visibly "puts on" His strength to defend His people. [3]
  - NET: strength is pictured as a belt that supports His rule. [10]
- **"The world is established."**
  - Calvin: since God made the world, He will not abandon it. Looking at the world is enough to show God's providence. [4]
  - Barnes: the comfort is that what God has set up is stable, even when disaster looms. [6]
  - Constable: the point is life on earth, not the planet as an object in space. [6]
  - Henry: if God keeps the world firm, He will keep His church firm all the more. [8]
- **Catholic reading (Augustine).** His Latin text reads "clothed with beauty." [11]
  - God put on beauty toward those who please Him and strength toward those who don't.
  - The "girding" points to Christ tying on a towel to wash the disciples' feet, so God's strength lies in humility.
  - The "world that cannot be moved" is the faithful spread across the whole earth.
  - His heading for the psalm: "on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded." He links it to the sixth day of creation and to Christ coming in the "sixth age."
- **Orthodox use.** Verse 1 ("The Lord is King: He is robed in majesty") is the Saturday-evening prokeimenon, a verse sung before the readings at Vespers. Orthodox Bibles number this psalm 92. [12]

**v. 2**
- Calvin reads the two halves as one thought: as God is eternal, so His throne has stood from eternity. Reading it as a simple statement that God is eternal is, he says, too thin. [4]
- NET agrees that "from antiquity [are] you" here refers to God's royal position, not just His existence. [10]
- Maclaren: "of old" is literally "from then," meaning the throne existed before any point in time. [7]
- Hengstenberg (via the Homiletical Commentary): the throne of wickedness has no "then"; it sprang up yesterday, like a mushroom. [9]
- Henry: God's right to rule rests on His having made the world. [8]
- Guzik: rebels oppose God's rule but have no chance of succeeding. [1]
- H.B. Charles: God is "no upstart despot." His kingdom did not begin when Israel became a nation. [13]
- Augustine applies "You are from everlasting" to Christ: though He was born in time, He is eternal. [11]

**v. 3**
- **The waters as God's enemies (the majority view).**
  - Spurgeon: the repetition shows how often and how violently the wicked attack God's rule, and how often they are beaten. "Voice" means furious words; "waves" means violent acts. [2]
  - Treasury of David: rivers bursting their banks picture invading armies. [2]
  - Henry: the waves picture raging nations (Isa 57:20; Ps 2:1). He adds an application to the storms of passion and fear inside our own hearts. [6][8]
  - NET: the waters stand for God's hostile enemies who try to destroy the order He set up. [10]
- **Calvin's caution.** He lists the "enemies of the Church" reading and a literal reading. He prefers the literal one: the roaring sea is one vivid example of God's terrifying power, as thunder is in Ps 29. [4] (This is a real difference in emphasis from Spurgeon and Henry.)
- **The rivers as empires.** Coffman (quoting another writer): the sea stands for the Gentile world, and the rivers for empires: the Nile for Egypt, the Tigris for Assyria, the Euphrates for Babylon. [5]
- **Ancient background.**
  - Constable: the Canaanites believed Baal defeated the sea god Yamm, so early readers would have heard this psalm as an argument against Baal worship. [6]
  - Bible Hub's Q&A: across the ancient Near East, floodwaters stood for chaos. The psalm takes over that picture to exalt Yahweh alone. [14]
  - Coffman pushes back: some commentators "find" Babylonian myth that isn't in the text, and Israel was not much shaped by it. [5]
- **Augustine's reading.** The "rivers" are the apostles, filled with the Spirit, lifting up their voices to preach. The raging sea is the persecution that followed. [11]

**v. 4**
- Spurgeon: God calls the waters' power a mere "noise," in contempt. "On high" means dominion, not location (Geier, quoted). [2]
- Barnes notes how fast the Hebrew moves here: the waters go only as far as God allows. [6]
- Clarke: God is stronger than all the peoples and nations who rise against Him. [6]
- Henry: "on high" means both God's safety (the waves can't reach Him) and His rule over them. [8]
- NET renders it "the LORD sits enthroned in majesty." [10]
- Treasury of David: the calming of the storm on Galilee pictures the history of God's kingdom. The believer's greatest dangers are only waves that break at God's feet. [2]
- H.B. Charles cites Ps 29:10: God reigns when the flood comes, not only when the sun shines. [13]
- Augustine: the boat is the Church and the sea is the world. Christ walks over the waves, and rulers and kings came to believe in Him. [11]

**v. 5**
- **"Testimonies" (God's word).**
  - Spurgeon: as God's throne is fixed in providence, His truth is beyond question in revelation. Literally the words are "very Amen-ed." [2]
  - Calvin: here the psalm turns from creation to God's special goodness in giving His saving teaching (the law) to His chosen people. [4]
  - Coffman: the testimonies include warnings, commands, promises and prophecies, all fully trustworthy. [5]
  - Maclaren: power is worth trusting only if it is gracious and makes itself known; words are worth trusting only if power stands behind them. [7]
- **"Holiness adorns Your house" (a real interpretive split).**
  - Maclaren: holiness here describes God's house itself, not the people who worship there. [7]
  - Coffman applies it to believers: God's family must not be defiled, and believers must keep striving to be holy (Heb 12:14). [5]
  - Spurgeon is in between: holiness is the result of the psalm's teaching, since honouring the King leads to conduct fit for His presence. [2]
  - Bible Hub's summary: holiness is the atmosphere of God's house and the calling of His people (1 Pet 1:15–16). [16]
  - Calvin: the "house" is the Church, where God placed the covenant of eternal life. [4]
- **"For all the days to come."**
  - Guzik: God's character does not fade with time. [1]
  - Bible.org notes that in Hebrew the "established" verbs in vv. 1–2 describe an ongoing, present-to-future state. [15]
- **Catholic and Orthodox.**
  - Augustine: the Lord's house will stand throughout the world and will not be moved, "unto length of days." [11]
  - The Orthodox sing "Holiness befits Thy house, O Lord, forevermore!" as one of the verses at Saturday Vespers. [12]

---

**Where the traditions differ (from the sources I found)**
- **Reformed (Calvin):** reads the floods literally, as a display of God's power, and the "house" as the Church that holds the covenant. [4]
- **Baptist (Spurgeon):** reads the floods as attacks on God's rule and the testimonies as an infallible revelation. [2]
- **Dispensational (Constable):** reads the psalm as pointing ahead to a millennial reign. [6]
- **Churches of Christ (Coffman):** reads "holiness" as a duty for worshippers and rejects the idea that the imagery comes from myth. [5]

I found no denomination-specific readings beyond these four.
